title: Given an array of non-negative house values, find the maximum amount you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses.
shortTitle: House Robber: cannot rob adjacent houses

s1_definition.oneliner: At each house, take the maximum of skipping it (best so far) or robbing it (its value plus the best from two positions back).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **House Robber** – a one-dimensional decision DP where each element has a binary choice: take or skip.
- **Recurrence** – `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2])`, encoding that robbing house i forbids house i-1.
- **Rolling variables** – since dp[i] depends only on the two preceding values, two variables replace the full array.
- **Time** – O(n) with a single pass through the array.
- **Space** – O(1) when using two rolling variables instead of an array.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India selects non-adjacent time slots for high-value promotional campaigns. Two back-to-back slots conflict because customers get fatigued. At each slot, the bank either skips it and keeps the best revenue so far, or takes it and adds its value to the best revenue from two slots ago. Whichever is larger becomes the new running best.

sections.s6_takeaway:
House Robber is a one-dimensional decision DP. At each house you face a binary choice: skip it, in which case the best total is whatever you had through the previous house, or rob it, in which case you earn its value plus the best total from two houses back, because robbing it forbids the immediately adjacent house. The recurrence is `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2])`.

Since each state depends only on the two preceding values, you keep two rolling variables rather than an array, giving linear time and constant space. The subtle point interviewers probe is why robbing reaches back two positions rather than one, and the answer is precisely the adjacency constraint: taking house i blocks house i-1, so the most recent safe state is house i-2.

In the National Bank of India project, marketing chose non-adjacent promotional time slots to maximize total campaign revenue, since consecutive slots would fatigue customers. This is structurally identical to House Robber. For the circular case (House Robber II), where the first and last slots are also adjacent, Rajesh ran the linear solution twice, once excluding the first slot and once excluding the last, and took the larger result.

The senior insight is that House Robber is a template for all non-adjacent selection problems. The same `max(skip, take + lookback)` pattern recurs in job scheduling, interval selection, and any problem where choosing one element excludes its neighbours. Recognising this pattern and reducing space with rolling variables is what interviewers expect at the senior level.

Remember one sentence: House Robber decides at each position whether to skip (carry forward dp[i-1]) or take (value plus dp[i-2]), and rolling two variables gives O(n) time and O(1) space.

---

keyPoints: Recurrence is dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2]) encoding the adjacency constraint.
Base cases are dp[0] = nums[0] and dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1]).
Rolling two variables replaces the array for O(1) space.
Circular variant (House Robber II) runs two linear passes excluding first or last house.
Time complexity is O(n) with a single pass through the array.
Template pattern for all non-adjacent selection problems.
